# 2 Kings 7 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1 — Elisha’s Prophecy of Plenty

**Traditional Reading (Evangelical Consensus):**

- **“Hear the word of the LORD”** is a solemn prophetic formula. Elisha speaks directly to the king (Jehoram/Joram) and his attendants, immediately after the king had blamed God for the famine and sought Elisha’s life (2 Kings 6:31–33). God responds to the king’s hostility with a word of grace — good news, not judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **“Tomorrow about this time”** — the prophecy is strikingly specific: within 24 hours, the famine would be completely reversed. This specificity would later serve as proof of Elisha’s prophetic authenticity (Deut 18:21–22). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **The prices**: A seah (about 7 quarts / 7.3 litres) of fine flour for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel. These prices were not “cheap” by normal standards (Patterson and Austel note they were “at a substantial price”), but they represented a dramatic collapse from the famine prices of 80 shekels for a donkey’s head and 5 shekels for dove’s dung (2 Kings 6:25). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **“In the gate of Samaria”** — the city gate was the marketplace and civic centre. Elisha’s prophecy envisions normal commerce resuming right where the siege had concentrated despair. The enemy was at the gate, but God would make it the place of life and provision again. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **Gill** notes the “seah” measure was about a gallon and a half (or two wine gallons and a half, per Bishop Cumberland), and a shekel about two shillings and fourpence farthing. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary**: Jehoram “appears to have accepted the prophet’s solemn asseveration, and on the strength of it to have spared his life, at any rate till the result should be seen.” (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm)

- **God’s grace to idolatrous Israel**: Precept Austin stresses that Yahweh gives this word of encouragement to a people who do not deserve it — the northern kingdom was worshipping Baal. Yahweh shows Himself the true source of fertility, not Baal. This is “amazing mercy mixed with pure grace.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

---

## v. 2 — The Officer’s Doubt and Elisha’s Judgment

**Traditional Reading:**

- **“The officer on whose arm the king leaned”** — the Hebrew word often translated “lord” or “captain” (שׁלישׁ, *shalish*) designates a high-ranking officer, the king’s right-hand man and third in rank. The leaning was literal — a custom of royal courts (cf. 2 Kings 5:18; 7:17). (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **“Windows in heaven”** — the officer’s sarcasm alludes to the flood narrative (Genesis 7:11), implying that even if God opened the heavens as in Noah’s day, such abundance could not arrive in 24 hours. He doubted God’s power, creativity, *and* messenger. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **Morgan** (cited by Guzik): “How often faith breaks down in this way! It knows that God is, and that He can act. But it only sees one way, and refuses to believe that such a way will be taken. The supply came without the opening of heaven’s windows.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **Guzik** lists six characteristics of unbelief illustrated by the officer: (1) dares to question the truthfulness of God’s promise; (2) says “this is new and cannot be true”; (3) says “this is sudden and cannot be true”; (4) says “there is no way”; (5) says “there is only one way God can work”; (6) says “even if God does something, it won’t be enough.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **“You shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it”** — Elisha pronounces a two-fold prophetic judgment. The officer would witness the miracle but not partake of it. This is both a threat and a warning, giving him time to repent. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Heightened accountability**: As a leading court official, the officer had witnessed Elisha’s previous miracles (the multiplied oil, the Shunammite’s son, Naaman’s healing, the blinded Aramean army). His unbelief was willful, not ignorant. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

**Baptist View (Spurgeon):**

- Spurgeon preached on this verse in “The Sin of Unbelief” (No. 3, 1855). He notes: “We hear not that any of the common people, the plebeians, ever did so; but an aristocrat did it. Strange it is, that God has seldom chosen the great men of this world. High places and faith in Christ do seldom well agree.” The officer’s sin lay in disbelieving after “repeated seals of Elisha’s ministry.” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-sin-of-unbelief)

- Spurgeon expands the application: “Unbelievers do not really enjoy the things of this life. The mass of them find that wealth does not yield them satisfaction, their outward riches cannot conceal their inner poverty. To many men it is given to have all that heart can wish, and yet not to have what their heart does wish. They have everything except contentment.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

**Baptist View (Garner-Howes):**

- “It is such unbelievers today who deny God and mock His coming (2 Peter 3:3-4).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

**Reformed View (Wiersbe, cited by Precept Austin):**

- “To the humble heart that’s open to God, the word generates faith, but to the proud, self-centered heart, the word makes the heart even harder. The same sun that melts the ice will harden the clay.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

---

## vv. 3–5 — The Four Lepers’ Decision

**Traditional Reading:**

- **“Four men with leprosy at the entrance of the city gate”** — lepers were excluded from cities by the Law (Leviticus 13:46; Numbers 5:3). They normally depended on food brought by family, but the famine meant no supplies reached them. They were the lowest of outcasts, yet God would use them as the unlikely messengers of deliverance. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **Jewish tradition** (noted by Gill and Guzik): these four were Gehazi and his three sons (Gehazi was struck with leprosy for his greed toward Naaman, 2 Kings 5:27). This is unfounded but interesting. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **“Why just sit here until we die?”** — their logic was flawless. Three options, all with the same likely outcome (death), but one offered a slim hope. If they entered the city, they would die of famine there. If they stayed, they would also die. Surrendering to the Syrians was the only path that *might* lead to survival (v. 4). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

- **“They arose at twilight”** — the evening twilight. They moved at dusk, perhaps to avoid detection from the city walls or to approach the Aramean camp under cover of darkness. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **“There was not a man to be found”** (v. 5) — the camp was completely deserted. Guzik notes they came to the “uttermost part” (the far side, away from the city), approaching as if from outside, to minimise risk. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

**Baptist View (Spurgeon, “The Sinner’s Only Alternative”):**

- Spurgeon draws the gospel analogy: “You perceive that there are just two courses open to you; you can sit still, but then you know that you must perish; or you can go to Christ, and your fear is that you will perish then. Yet you can but die if you go to him, and he rejects you; whereas, if you do not go to him, you must surely perish.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

**Baptist View (Garner-Howes):**

- Applies the lepers’ reasoning as an analogy both for the lost (who have nothing to lose by coming to Christ) and for saved believers wasting their lives in worldliness (1 Corinthians 3:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

---

## vv. 6–7 — God’s Miraculous Panic of the Arameans

**Traditional Reading:**

- **“The LORD had caused the Arameans to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army”** — God attacked the Syrian army through auditory illusion. Guzik draws a parallel with 2 Kings 6: the God who struck one Syrian army with blindness now struck another with phantom sounds. Whether God put actual noise into the air or created the perception in their minds, the result was the same. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **Patterson and Austel** (cited by Guzik) suggest the lepers’ stumbling footsteps may have been magnified by God to sound like an army, providing the occasion for the miracle. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **“The king of Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and Egyptians”** — historically, the Hittite empire had collapsed centuries earlier, but neo-Hittite city-states still existed in northern Syria. Egypt, though diminished, was still a military power. The Syrians’ panic made them imagine the most unlikely alliance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Gill**: the panic was either “by the ministry of angels” or God working on their imagination. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **“They fled at twilight”** (v. 7) — the same twilight when the lepers set out. God’s timing was perfectly coordinated; the lepers and Syrians moved simultaneously, each unaware of the other’s movement. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **“The camp was intact”** — the Syrians fled in such terror that they left tents, horses, donkeys, and all supplies untouched. The untouched camp demonstrated that no human battle had occurred — this was purely God’s work. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

**Baptist View (Spurgeon, “Who Found It Out?”):**

- “Everybody who went to bed that night felt that he was still in that horrible den where grim death seemed actually present in the skeleton forms of the hunger-bitten. They were as free as the harts of the wilderness had they known it: but their ignorance held them in vile durance [imprisonment].” The deliverance was real, but the people inside Samaria did not yet know it. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/who-found-it-out)

**Garner-Howes:** Notes that “the Lord had told Israel generations earlier how He would make their enemies fear and flee, but they turned from Him. He shows them His verity and faithfulness in caring for them in spite of their disobedience (Proverbs 28:1; Job 15:21).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

---

## vv. 8–9 — The Lepers Feast, Hoard, Then Repent

**Traditional Reading:**

- **v. 8 — Eating, drinking, and hiding valuables**: The lepers’ first act was to satisfy their hunger — entirely natural after prolonged famine. Then they took silver, gold, and clothing, hid them, and repeated the process in another tent. Guzik notes this is understandable: they knew the camp would be discovered eventually and wanted to secure their own provision. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **v. 9 — “We are not doing what is right”**: Spurgeon’s key point here is that the lepers first enjoyed the provision themselves before telling others: “They did that which it was right to do; they fed themselves; but then they felt that they must not keep the good things to themselves.” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/public-testimony-a-debt-to-god-and-man)

- **“This day is a day of good news”** (Hebrew: *besorah*; LXX: *euaggelia*) — Precept Austin notes this is literally “a gospel day.” The lepers recognised that keeping silent would be sin. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **“Some punishment will come upon us”** — the lepers feared either divine judgment or human retribution (from the king or the returning Syrians) if they withheld the news. Gill notes the possible fear of “some evil from the immediate hand of God.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Guzik**: “They understood that to remain silent and to selfishly enjoy their blessings would be sin. They had a responsibility to share the good news.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

**Baptist View (Spurgeon, “Public Testimony: A Debt to God and Man”):**

- “If the only result of our religion is the comfort of our poor little souls, if the beginning and the end of piety is contained within one’s self, why, it is a strange thing to be in connection with the unselfish Jesus, and to be the fruit of his gracious Spirit. Surely, Jesus did not come to save us that we might live unto ourselves. He came to save us from selfishness.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- Spurgeon also stresses that we should first “taste and see that the Lord is good” before we can testify with conviction: “If any say to you, ‘Are you sure that it is true?’ you will answer, ‘Ay, that I am, for I have tasted and handled of the good word of life.’” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/public-testimony-a-debt-to-god-and-man)

**Baptist View (Garner-Howes):**

- Applies this as a sermon on evangelistic responsibility: “God’s people do not well if they serve themselves instead of spreading the good news of salvation. Their lifetime on earth as God’s children is a day of good tidings, and yet many hold their peace.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

**Grant’s Commentary (Brethren):**

- “We who are believers in the Lord Jesus might well take a serious lesson from this. We have been infinitely blessed by the gospel of God’s salvation. Are we doing right if we conceal it from others?” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-kings-7.html — from search excerpt)

---

## vv. 10–11 — The Lepers Report to the Gatekeepers

**Traditional Reading:**

- **“They called out to the gatekeepers”**: The lepers could not enter the city. They communicated what they could to whom they could — the gatekeepers. The good news then passed from person to person until it reached the king’s household. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- Their report emphasised: no one there, only tethered animals, tents intact — exactly what they had witnessed. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Guzik**: “There were many people they could not speak to, but they were faithful to speak to the ones they could speak to.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

---

## vv. 12–15 — The King’s Suspicion and the Scouts’ Confirmation

**Traditional Reading:**

- **v. 12 — The king’s suspicion**: Jehoram assumed a military stratagem — that the Syrians were hiding in ambush to lure the starving Israelites out. This was tactically plausible but spiritually blind. Garner-Howes calls Jehoram “one of the most pessimistic, sin-hardened men who ever lived, when it came to acknowledging the power of God.” He had “evidently already forgotten the prediction of the man of God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

- **v. 13 — The servant’s wise counsel**: One servant urged sending scouts with five of the remaining horses. His argument: even if the horses and riders were lost, their fate would be no worse than the mass of Israelites already dying. The risk was worth taking. Gill notes these horses were starving anyway. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

- **v. 14 — Two chariots sent**: The king compromised — not five horses but two chariots. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **v. 15 — The trail of discarded items**: The scouts tracked the Syrians all the way to the Jordan River. The road was littered with garments and equipment thrown off in panic. This confirmed a genuine, headlong flight, not an organised ambush. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Gill**: “Garments” and “vessels” (weapons/armour, per Josephus) were thrown away “for quicker dispatch.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

---

## v. 16 — The Prophecy Fulfilled

**Traditional Reading:**

- **The people plundered the camp**: Once confirmed, there was no holding back the starving population. They poured out to seize food and riches. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

- **The exact prices**: A seah of fine flour for a shekel, two seahs of barley for a shekel — precisely as Elisha had spoken. This validated Elisha as a true prophet per Deuteronomy 18:21–22. The prophecy was “not vague, general, or distant—it was specific in content, timing, and outcome.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **Meyer** (cited by Guzik): The king’s officer “derided the possibility of the prophet’s prediction; and no doubt had plenty of adherents. But the lepers’ report swept away all his words to the winds. They had known, tasted, and handled.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-7/)

---

## vv. 17–20 — The Death of the Doubting Officer

**Traditional Reading:**

- **v. 17 — Appointment to the gate and death by trampling**: The king appointed the doubting officer to supervise the gate — perhaps as a rebuke, forcing him to personally manage the very provision he said could never come. The starving crowd, desperate for food, trampled him. Whether the death was accidental (the crush of the crowd) or violent (resistance to his authority) is debated. Bähr thought it accidental; Pulpit Commentary agrees the text is compatible with an accidental death, noting “such deaths are not uncommon in dense crowds.” (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm)

- **Gill**: The officer was placed “to prevent disorders and tumults among the people” or “to regulate the market,” but “through the people’s pressing to get provisions, he was overborne, and trod upon.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/7.htm)

- **vv. 18–20 — The repetition for emphasis**: The narrator repeats both Elisha’s prophecy and the officer’s scoffing words verbatim before recording the fulfilment. This literary technique (“with obvious satisfaction,” says Ellicott) underscores God’s absolute reliability and the certainty of judgment on proud unbelief. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/7.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-7-commentary)

- **The officer saw but did not eat**: He witnessed the prices drop, but “did not, in his own person, obtain any benefit from the sudden plenty, since he perished before he could profit by it.” (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_kings/7.htm)

**Spurgeon (“The Sin of Unbelief”):**

- “Providence — which always fulfills prophecy, just as the paper takes the stamp of the type — destroyed the man. Trodden down in the streets of Samaria, he perished at its gates, beholding the plenty, but tasting not of it.” (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-sin-of-unbelief — from search excerpt)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):**

- Draws an analogy with the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31): “When it was too late to do anything about it he saw the salvation, but died without it… Too late people will lift up their eyes in torment and see all the good things they might have had.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-7.html)

---

## Summary of Where Protestant Traditions Differ

From the sources accessed:

- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Garner-Howes)**: Strong emphasis on evangelistic application — the lepers as a type of the sinner who must venture on Christ, and the believer’s duty to share the gospel. Spurgeon also stresses God’s sovereignty in choosing unlikely instruments (lepers, not nobles). The officer’s unbelief is treated as a warning to the self-righteous and the privileged who reject clear evidence.

- **Reformed (Wiersbe, via Precept Austin)**: Emphasis on the sovereignty of God’s word — the same word that hardens the proud (the officer) brings life to the humble (the lepers). The “windows in heaven” scoffing is treated as a theological error about God’s power and freedom to work outside human expectations.

- **Charismatic/Pentecostal (Enduring Word/David Guzik)**: Guzik is broadly evangelical but is widely used in charismatic circles. His emphasis on God’s “creativity” in providing unexpectedly, the immediacy of the turnaround (“When everything screams ‘impossible’ God’s Word says ‘possible’”), and the importance of personal testimony (“we cannot properly share the good news of Jesus Christ unless we ourselves are enjoying it”) resonates with charismatic emphases on personal experience and the power of testimony.

- **Brethren (Grant’s Commentary)**: Emphasis on grace — God’s provision despite the king’s unworthiness, and the responsibility of believers who have received blessing to share it.

*Note: I was unable to access distinctively Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu), or Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) commentaries within the tool limits. No prosperity/Word of Faith specific teaching on this chapter was found in the sources searched. No modern scholarly sources (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) were accessible.*

## Cross-References and Themes

- **2 Kings 6:24–33**: The immediate context — the siege, the cannibalism, the king’s rage against Elisha.
- **Genesis 7:11**: The “windows of heaven” language alludes to the flood.
- **Malachi 3:10**: God promises to open the windows of heaven and pour out blessing — a positive use of the same imagery that the officer scoffed at.
- **Deuteronomy 18:21–22**: The test of a true prophet — exact fulfilment validates Elisha.
- **Psalm 78:19–21, 41**: Israel’s history of doubting God’s ability to provide, which the officer’s scoffing echoes.
- **Revelation 6:6**: The famine conditions of the third seal — a seah of wheat for a denarius — echo the economic language of this chapter.
